body: How do you combine your WSET course with self-study?

Use the course for first contact with each topic and your own study for everything that makes it stick: a short preview before each class, questions and flashcards within 24 hours after it, and a weekly mixed review. The course sets the pace; self-study decides how much of it you still remember on exam day.

WSET courses come in very different shapes. Some run as one evening a week for two months, others as two or three intensive days, others again as online programmes you follow at your own pace with a tutor available for questions. The right self-study routine depends on which shape you have, because the risk is different in each case: with a weekly class you forget between sessions, with an intensive course you receive too much at once, and with an online course nothing forces you to keep going.
How to organise your own study
Forgetting the previous class before the next one
Questions on the new chapter the day after class, flashcards every day, a mixed set at the weekend
Intensive course of two or three days
Too much information in too little time
Read the first chapters before the course, then use the weeks between the course and the exam for questions, flashcards and mocks
Online course at your own pace
Book the exam first, then build a study plan backwards from that date with a daily goal
Restart with mixed questions to find gaps, then move into regular timed mocks

Whatever your format, a ten-minute preview before a class pays off. Skim the chapter headings, look at a map of the region or a diagram of the process, and answer five questions even if you get them wrong. You will arrive with questions of your own, and the class will answer them instead of washing over you.

There is no single correct way to prepare: the same method has to fit a full-time job, a family or irregular shifts. These three typical situations show how the principles on this page translate into real weeks.
Six weeks to Level 2, with a full-time office job

A candidate with an office job and a Level 2 exam six weeks away has about 30 to 40 minutes a day and a longer slot at weekends. The plan that works is boring on purpose: flashcards on the commute, one lesson or 20 practice questions in the evening, and one longer session on Saturday for a mixed set and the mistakes review. The first full mock goes in at week four, the second at week five, the third early in week six. Nothing is crammed, so the final week is mostly review and rest.
Three months to Level 3, with young children

A parent preparing Level 3 rarely gets a quiet hour, but often gets three quiet twenty-minute blocks. The trick is to give each block a single job: one for flashcards and questions, one for a lesson, one for writing a short answer or a tasting note. Tasting happens at dinner with whatever wine is open, described aloud with the systematic approach. Weekends hold the timed elements, such as a written-answer set or a theory mock, when a partner can cover the household for two hours.
Spirits Level 2, around evening bar shifts

A bartender working late shifts studies best in the early afternoon before work and in short bursts during quiet moments. Spirits Level 2 rewards this: the principal spirits carry the most questions, and the bar itself is a revision tool. Every bottle on the back bar becomes a flashcard prompt (raw material, still type, ageing rules), and cocktails become a quick check of service knowledge. Mock exams go on days off, in the morning, when concentration is highest.
A handful of terms come up again and again in WSET preparation. Knowing exactly what each one means makes course materials, exam instructions and feedback much easier to follow.
The total time, including class hours, that a typical learner needs to prepare a level; a minimum to plan around, not a promise
No notes, textbook or devices in the exam room; everything must come from memory
The question part of a multiple-choice item, before the options; the key word is usually here
A wrong option written to look plausible, such as a real grape from the wrong region
A separately assessed part of a qualification; at Wine Level 3 the theory and the tasting are two units
The specific ideas an examiner gives marks for in a written answer
The verb that tells you what to do in a written question: describe, explain, compare
The structured method for describing appearance, nose, palate and conclusions in exam vocabulary
Higher grades above a pass: at Level 2, 70% and 85%
A full practice paper with the real number of questions and the real time limit
Are you ready for the exam? A readiness checklist

You are ready when your mock scores are consistently above your target grade, your list of recurring mistakes is short, and no chapter feels like a blind spot. Use this checklist in the last ten days; every "no" is a revision task, not a reason to panic.
I have studied every chapter of the syllabus at least once, including the short ones at the end.
My last two timed mock exams were above my target grade, not just above the pass mark.
My weakest chapter in the last mock was still at or close to the pass mark.
I can name the grape or raw material behind every region or category I studied without hesitating.
I know the label terms and key numbers of my level well enough to answer in a few seconds.
I finished my last mock with time to spare and checked my flagged questions.
At Level 3, I have written at least a dozen short answers under time pressure and marked them honestly.
At Level 3, I can write a complete tasting note for two wines in the time allowed.
I know the date, time, place or online set-up of my exam and what my course provider asks me to bring.
If two or more boxes stay empty a week before the exam, do not add new material. Spend the remaining days on exactly those gaps, with short targeted sessions and one last mock.
Can you prepare for a wine and a spirits level at the same time?

You can, but it works best when the two exams are a few weeks apart and you give each one its own daily slot. Studying both in parallel without a plan tends to blur facts that look alike, such as ageing terms used in both worlds.

The two pathways share useful foundations: tasting technique, the effect of oak, the idea of protected names and label rules. They also contain look-alike vocabulary that causes confusion, for example "Reserva" on a Spanish wine label and age statements on spirits labels, which follow very different rules. If you prepare both, keep separate flashcard decks, take the earlier exam first and use the weeks after it to switch your daily goal to the second level.
faq: Is the WSET exam open book?

No. WSET exams are closed-book: you cannot use notes, textbooks or devices during the paper. That is why active recall matters so much in your preparation. Answering questions from memory, reviewing flashcards and sitting timed mocks without notes train exactly the skill the exam tests, while rereading only makes the material feel familiar. Practise without looking anything up, then check your answers afterwards.
Can I prepare for WSET without taking a course?

You can do much of the learning on your own, but you still enrol with a WSET course provider to sit the exam, and many providers include the course with the exam. Self-study works best as a complement: the course gives you the structure, a tutor and guided tastings, while an app like The Wine Goat gives you the daily practice, flashcards and mock exams that make the content stick until exam day.
How do I stay motivated during WSET preparation?

Make the daily goal small enough to meet on a bad day, track your streak and chapter progress, and connect study to real bottles you open or serve. Seeing a weak chapter move from 50% to 80% in practice questions is far more motivating than counting hours. If motivation drops, shorten sessions rather than skipping them: ten minutes of flashcards keeps the habit and the memory alive.
What should I do the morning of a WSET exam?

Keep it light. Eat normally, review a short set of flashcards or your list of personal confusions for ten to fifteen minutes, then stop. Check the time, place or online set-up and what your course provider asks you to bring. Arrive or log in early so you start calm. Avoid learning anything new: last-minute details tend to push out facts you already knew well.
Is it better to study in the morning or the evening?

Study when you are most alert and least likely to be interrupted, and keep that slot consistent. Many people find mornings better for new lessons and mock exams, and evenings fine for flashcards and short question sets. If you can, sit at least one mock exam at the same time of day as your real exam, so your concentration is trained for that moment.

body: One topic, three levels: how the depth changes
The clearest way to see the difference between the levels is to follow one topic through all three. The facts overlap, but Level 1 asks what, Level 2 asks what and where, and Level 3 asks why.
Is it a white or a black grape, and what does it taste like?
How does Chablis differ from a warm-climate Chardonnay, and which regions grow it?
Explain how climate, malolactic conversion, lees and oak shape the styles of Chardonnay
What is sparkling wine, and how should it be served?
Which method makes Champagne and which makes Prosecco?
Explain how the method and time on lees affect the style and price of a sparkling wine
Do cool and warm climates make different styles?
Which regions are cool or warm, and what styles do they give?
Explain how latitude, altitude, water and diurnal range change ripening
What do the main words on a label tell you?
What do terms such as Riserva, Crianza or Kabinett mean?
How do quality categories and legal rules relate to style and quality?

Use this ladder to check where you are. If you can already answer the Level 2 column with confidence, Level 2 will feel like consolidation and you may be ready to plan for Level 3. If even the Level 1 column feels uncertain, a short Level 1 preparation will make everything after it easier.
A glossary of wine terms you meet at every level
These terms appear across the wine levels, with growing precision. Learn a one-line definition early and add detail as you move up.
The overall sense of weight and richness of a wine in the mouth, mostly from alcohol and sugar
A compound from grape skins, seeds and oak that gives red wines a drying, grippy feel
The fresh, mouth-watering element of a wine; cool climates generally keep more of it
A process that turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, sometimes with buttery notes
Dead yeast cells left after fermentation; contact with them adds texture and bready or biscuit notes
Sparkling wine made by a second fermentation in the bottle, as in Champagne
Sparkling wine made by a second fermentation in a sealed tank, as for most Prosecco
Adding grape spirit to wine, during or after fermentation, as for Port and Sherry
A fungus that concentrates sugar in grapes and is behind some famous sweet wines
The difference between day and night temperatures; cool nights help keep acidity
A legally defined place name with rules on grapes, yields and winemaking
Shorthand for the traditional European regions and the regions outside Europe
Moving up a level: what changes in the way you study
Each step up asks for a new study skill, not just more facts. Changing the way you study at the start of the new level saves weeks of frustration.

At Level 1, a list of eight grapes and a few rules is enough. At Level 2 the volume of names multiplies, and the challenge becomes organisation. Stop learning grapes and regions as separate lists and start building pairs and grids: a region always comes with its grape, its climate and its typical style. Flashcards become essential at this point, because recognition alone will not separate two regions in the same country.

Level 3 adds two new skills: writing explanations and tasting accurately. Many strong Level 2 candidates are surprised by their first written answers, which tend to be lists of correct words without the reasons that earn the marks. Start writing short answers in the first weeks, not after you finish the regions. Do the same with tasting: one structured note per wine you drink, with the exam vocabulary, is worth more than an occasional long tasting session.
Before you start the next level
Keep your flashcards from the previous level and review them weekly: Level 3 assumes everything from Level 2.
Revisit the vineyard and winemaking basics before you meet the new regions.
Taste a few classic wines you studied, so names become real flavours.
Set the exam date early, so your plan has a clear end point.
Choosing a level: three typical situations
Real decisions depend on background, goals and time. These short examples show how candidates usually decide.
A new restaurant server who wants to talk confidently about the wine list in a month: Level 2, with Level 1 skipped, because the regions and label terms on a wine list are Level 2 content.
An enthusiast who has enjoyed wine for years but never studied it, with only two free weekends: Level 1 now, then Level 2 when there is time for several weeks of regular study.
A shop assistant who passed Level 2 with merit and is starting to advise customers on fine wine: Level 3, planned over about three months, with tasting built into every week.
A career changer aiming at buying or education roles: Level 2 and Level 3 in sequence, keeping in mind that the Diploma usually follows for those paths.
If you cannot decide between two levels, look at the practice questions for the higher one. If you can answer around half of them before studying, that level is a realistic target.
faq: Can I take WSET Wine Level 3 without Level 2?

Level 3 recommends Level 2 or equivalent knowledge, and some course providers may accept proven experience instead. In practice, skipping Level 2 is rarely wise: Level 3 assumes you already know the principal grapes, regions and label terms, and spends its time on explaining why. If you want to test yourself, try Level 2 practice questions first; frequent gaps there are a sign to build those foundations before Level 3.
Is there a tasting exam at WSET Wine Level 2?

No. Wine Level 2 is assessed only by 50 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes. Tasting is still part of the course and helps you remember styles, because a grape you have tasted is easier to recall than one you have only read about. Writing short notes with the systematic approach at Level 2 is also good training if you plan to continue to Level 3, where tasting has its own unit.
How much time should I leave between Level 2 and Level 3?

There is no fixed rule. Some candidates move on within a few weeks while Level 2 knowledge is fresh, others take a few months to gain tasting experience. What matters is that Level 2 content is still secure when you start: review your Level 2 flashcards and practice questions before the course, and plan two to three months of regular study for Level 3 itself.
Which grapes do I need to know for WSET Wine Level 2?

The eight principal grapes are central: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Syrah. Around these, Level 2 adds about 22 regionally important varieties linked to their key regions, such as Tempranillo in Rioja, Sangiovese in Chianti or Nebbiolo in Barolo. Learn each one with its regions, climate and typical style rather than as an isolated name.
Is WSET Wine Level 2 enough to work in a wine shop or restaurant?

For many roles in retail, service and wholesale, Level 2 gives a solid working foundation: you will understand the grapes, regions and label terms you meet every day. Employers' expectations vary, and roles involving buying, fine wine or training often look for Level 3. Whatever the role, combining the qualification with regular tasting of the wines you actually sell makes the knowledge useful straight away.

body: A worked example: reviewing a Level 2 mock

Imagine a Wine Level 2 candidate who scores 31 out of 50 (62%) on a first mock three weeks before the exam. That is a pass, but with almost no margin. The breakdown by topic shows where the next two weeks should go.
Contrast cards: Loire versus Burgundy whites, Northern versus Southern Rhône
Relearn the lesson, then 20 questions on the chapter
Slow down on stems with "main" and "typically"
Weakest chapter, left to the end
Two short sessions this week, then mixed questions
Rebuild the food and wine interaction table from memory

The total hides the story: almost half of the lost marks come from two chapters. After a week of targeted work on sparkling and fortified wines and on Italian and Spanish labels, a second mock at 37 out of 50 (74%) would put the candidate above the merit threshold with a real margin. That is the purpose of the first mock: not to judge, but to point.
Pacing plans for each exam format
Know your checkpoints before you start: where you should be at the halfway mark and how much time you keep for flagged questions. A pacing plan prevents both rushing and running out of time.
Time to keep at the end
Time is generous; use it to reread stems, not to rush
Answer easy questions in under a minute to bank time for harder ones
Decide your split before you start
A few minutes to reread written answers
Do not let the multiple-choice section eat the time the written answers need

At Level 3, the split between multiple choice and written answers is personal, but it must be decided in advance and practised. A common approach is to work through the multiple-choice questions at a steady pace, flag the doubtful ones, and give the written answers a fixed share of the time with a rough budget per question in proportion to its marks. Check your provider's instructions for the exact exam duration and rehearse with that number.
What your mock score tells you
Read a mock score as a range, not a promise: the real exam can be a few points higher or lower. The safer your margin above the threshold you want, the more confident you can be.
Not yet at the pass mark
Return to lessons on the weakest chapters, then chapter questions before the next mock
Targeted revision on two or three chapters; aim to gain 5 points in the next mock
Fix confusions and label terms; work on precision in reading the stem
Keep mocks weekly, review every error, and polish the small topics
How to mark your own Level 3 written mock

Mark your written answers against marking points, one idea at a time, and be strict: a mark only counts if the idea is correct, relevant to the question and explained. Self-marking is a skill in itself, and it improves quickly with practice.
Read the question again and note how many marks each part carries: that is roughly how many separate ideas you need.
Compare your answer with the model answer and its marking points, line by line.
Tick a point only if your sentence states it clearly; a keyword without the reason does not count.
Circle any idea you wrote that is correct but does not answer the question; it earns nothing and costs time.
Rewrite the weakest part in two or three sentences, then file it with your mistakes to revisit in a week.
Reading a Spirits Level 2 mock by section

The Spirits Level 2 paper is weighted towards the principal spirits, so review your mock by section and spend your time where the marks are. Of the 50 questions, 14 cover production, 23 the principal spirits, 7 flavoured spirits and aromatised wines, and 6 service and cocktails.
Pot versus column still, the effect of cask type and size
Draw each process from memory and explain each step's effect on style
Legal rules, minimum ageing, label terms
Flashcards for every number and term, then mixed questions by category
Group them into families and learn one example per family
Link each classic cocktail to its base spirit and family

Losing six marks on principal spirits is far more serious than losing two on cocktails, even if the cocktail mistakes feel more embarrassing. Let the weighting, not your feelings, decide the revision plan.
Mini case: one week to a Level 1 exam

A candidate with Wine or Spirits Level 1 in seven days and little time can still use mocks well. Day one: a first 30-question mock, untimed if needed, simply to see which chapters are weak. Days two to five: 15–20 minutes a day of lessons and questions on those chapters, plus flashcards. Day six: a second mock under real timing, 45 minutes, aiming well above 70%. Day seven: only flashcards and the list of mistakes. Two mocks, reviewed properly, are enough at this level.
faq: How do I simulate WSET exam conditions at home?

Choose a quiet place and a time you will not be interrupted, set the real time limit, and put away notes, books and your phone. Answer every question without pausing the clock. If your real exam is on a computer, practise on a screen; if it is on paper, try noting your answers by hand. Small details like these make the real day feel familiar.
What if my mock exam scores are getting worse?

First, check whether the mocks are comparable: a new mock may cover chapters you studied long ago, which is exactly what it should reveal. Look at the scores by chapter rather than the total. A drop usually comes from older topics fading, which means your flashcard and mixed-question reviews need more time. Fix those chapters, then sit another mock a few days later.
How long should I spend reviewing a mock exam?

At least as long as the mock itself: about an hour for a Level 2 mock, and more for Level 3 written answers. Go through every wrong answer and every lucky guess, classify the mistake, read the explanation and decide one concrete action for each topic. A rushed five-minute review wastes most of the value of the mock.
Should I take a mock exam the day before the real exam?

Usually not. A full mock the day before can tire you and shake your confidence if one score is lower than expected. Sit your last full mock two or three days before the exam, then use the final day for light flashcards and your list of personal confusions. Rest is part of the preparation.

body: Every multiple-choice question has three parts: a stem that asks the question, one key that answers it, and three distractors built from real facts used in the wrong place. Seeing the structure helps you read questions the way they were written.

Take a typical Level 2 item: "Which grape variety is mainly used for red Rioja?" The key is Tempranillo. The distractors might be Garnacha, which is genuinely grown in Rioja but is not the main grape; Nebbiolo, a famous black grape from the wrong country; and Malbec, a grape strongly associated with another region. Each wrong option tests a different confusion: a real partner grape, a real grape from another place, and a well-known name that sounds plausible. The word "mainly" is what turns Garnacha from tempting into wrong.
Four kinds of distractor, and how to beat them
Most wrong options fall into a few families. Recognising the family tells you what knowledge the question is really checking.
Sauvignon Blanc offered for a red Burgundy question
Learning regions and grapes as pairs, in both directions
Reading qualifiers such as main, typically, minimum
Learning each process with its effect, not just its name
A correct fact about Port in a question about Sherry
Checking that the option answers this stem, not just that it is true
These questions mix levels and include more demanding distractors. Answer each one before opening the explanation, and notice which kind of distractor tempted you.
Chianti Classico is mainly made from which grape variety?

Chianti, in Tuscany, is based on Sangiovese. Nebbiolo and Barbera are Piedmont grapes, and Montepulciano is a grape grown mainly in central and southern Italy, which makes it a classic "sounds like the region" trap.
What does the term "Brut" indicate on a sparkling wine label?
A wine made by the tank method
A wine aged at least five years
Brut is a sweetness term and indicates a dry style. It says nothing about the production method or the ageing period, which are what the other options describe.
Why are vineyards in cool regions of the Northern Hemisphere often planted on south-facing slopes?
To catch more sunlight and warmth
To protect the vines from rain
To reduce sugar in the grapes
South-facing slopes receive more direct sunlight in the Northern Hemisphere, helping grapes ripen in marginal climates. Better ripening increases sugar rather than reducing it.
Which winemaking technique is most associated with the fruity red wines of Beaujolais?

Whole bunches fermenting in a carbon dioxide-rich environment give the soft tannins and bright red-fruit, sometimes banana-like, aromas typical of many Beaujolais wines. Lees stirring is mainly a white winemaking technique.
Which type of still typically produces a lighter, more neutral spirit?
Neither; style depends only on the raw material
A column still allows continuous distillation to high strength, removing more flavour compounds and giving a lighter, more neutral spirit. Pot stills generally give fuller, more flavourful spirits.
Tequila is made from blue agave. Sugar cane is the raw material of rum, barley of many whiskies and grapes of brandy, each a real raw material for the wrong spirit.
What is the minimum ageing for Scotch whisky?
Three years in oak in Scotland
Scotch whisky must be matured in oak casks in Scotland for at least three years. The other options borrow numbers and rules that belong to other categories.
What is the main difference between a Fino and an Oloroso Sherry?
Fino is sweet, Oloroso is dry
Fino ages under a layer of flor, Oloroso ages oxidatively
Fino is made from black grapes

Fino matures under flor, a layer of yeast that protects it from oxygen and keeps it pale and fresh; Oloroso matures without flor, developing a darker colour and nutty flavours. Both are fortified and both are made dry.
How many practice questions does each level need?

Think in coverage, not in totals: every chapter should be practised several times, in chapter sets first and then in mixed sets. The figures below are a practical guide for planning, not a requirement.
A few hundred, covering every chapter more than once
Most of a full question bank, with mistakes repeated
A large bank across all regions, revisited in mixed sets

A Level 2 candidate has scored around 60% in mixed sets for two weeks. More questions alone have not helped. The fix starts with the data: sorting the last 100 wrong answers shows that a third are confusions between regions in the same country and a quarter are misread stems. The candidate builds ten contrast cards for the confused pairs, reads every stem twice for qualifiers, and practises in smaller, slower sets for a week. Mixed scores climb towards 70%, because the problem was never a lack of effort but a few repeated patterns.
faq: Are WSET multiple-choice questions designed to be tricky?

They are designed to be precise rather than tricky. Wrong options are usually real facts placed in the wrong context, so a vague memory is not enough. Read the full stem, look for qualifiers such as "main" or "minimum", predict the answer before reading the options and eliminate what does not fit. Candidates who learn grapes, regions and processes as linked pairs find most questions straightforward.
Should I start practice questions before I finish the course?

Yes. Start with questions on each chapter as soon as you have studied it, even in the first week. Early testing shows what did not stick while the lesson is still fresh, and it strengthens memory more than rereading. Leave full mixed mock exams for later, when you have covered most of the syllabus, but do not wait until the end to start testing yourself.
What practice score shows I am ready for the exam?

Look for consistent scores in mixed sets and mocks comfortably above the threshold you are aiming for. At Level 2, many candidates use about 70% in mixed practice as a sign of a safe pass, and around 85% or more for a realistic distinction attempt. Check chapter scores too: one very weak chapter can cost several marks on the day.
Can I practise WSET questions in my own language?

In The Wine Goat you can practise in English, Italian, French or Spanish, with separate versions for Spain and Argentina. A useful approach is to learn difficult concepts in the language you think in and then answer questions in the language of your exam, so the exact terminology becomes familiar before the day.
